title: Do Team and Individual Debriefs Enhance Performance? A Meta-Analysis
authors: Scott I. Tannenbaum; Christopher P. Cerasoli
key_findings: 46 samples (N=2,136): debriefs improve effectiveness over control by ~25% on average (d=.67)
Effects similar for teams and individuals, simulated and real settings, medical and non-medical samples
Alignment of participants, focus and level of measurement bolsters the effect; facilitation and structure may help
practical_applications: Run a short structured debrief after each job; align it to the unit that did the work
limitations: Mostly training/simulation settings; outcome is task performance, not long-term organisational learning

title: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of the after-action review (or debrief) and factors that influence its effectiveness
authors: Nathanael L. Keiser; Winfred Arthur Jr.
key_findings: 61 studies (107 ds; 915 teams, 3,499 individuals): overall d=0.79 across training criteria
Alignment (individual vs team) and objective performance review media consistently raise effectiveness
Facilitation effects interactive: self-led + team-aligned and self-led + objective media most effective; high structure helped in military, not in healthcare
practical_applications: Base the review on objective records (renders, metrics, the user's words), not memory

title: After-Event Reviews: Drawing Lessons From Successful and Failed Experience
authors: Shmuel Ellis; Inbar Davidi
key_findings: Soldiers debriefed on failures AND successes after each navigation day improved more than those reviewing failures only
Before the manipulation mental models of failed events were richer than of successful events; the gap closed with success reviews
practical_applications: Every review asks what worked and why; log approved works with their causes

title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
authors: K. Anders Ericsson; Ralf Th. Krampe; Clemens Tesch-Roemer
key_findings: Expert performance explained as the result of prolonged deliberate practice: effortful activities designed to improve performance
Individual differences even among elites closely related to assessed amounts of deliberate practice
practical_applications: Design practice that targets a weakness with feedback, not just more output
limitations: Retrospective practice estimates; core finding not replicated by Macnamara & Maitra 2019

title: Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Brooke N. Macnamara; David Z. Hambrick; Frederick L. Oswald
key_findings: Deliberate practice explained 26% of performance variance in games, 21% music, 18% sports, 4% education, <1% professions
Deliberate practice is important but not as important as argued
practical_applications: Do not promise that logging lessons alone makes a studio excellent; measure outcomes
limitations: Definition of deliberate practice disputed by Ericsson & Harwell 2019

title: The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Roemer (1993)
authors: Brooke N. Macnamara; Megha Maitra
key_findings: Double-blind replication did not replicate the core finding that accumulated deliberate practice corresponded to each violin skill level
Effect substantial but considerably smaller than original; teacher-designed practice did not explain more variance than practice alone
practical_applications: Treat the 10,000-hour story as contested

title: Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice on the Acquisition of Expert Performance
authors: K. Anders Ericsson; Kyle W. Harwell
key_findings: Argues Macnamara 2014 measured 'structured practice', not deliberate practice in the original sense (teacher-guided, individualised)
Reanalysis restricted to studies meeting their criteria: practice explains 29% and 61% (after attenuation correction)
practical_applications: Practice counts when goals are specific and feedback comes from a qualified source
limitations: Authors are the theory's originators; criteria chosen after the fact are open to dispute

title: Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
authors: Agnar Aamodt; Enric Plaza
key_findings: General CBR framework: case retrieval, reuse, solution testing (revise) and learning (retain)
CBR as one reasoning-and-learning method inside integrated architectures
practical_applications: Store each finished job as a case (problem, solution, outcome) and retrieve the nearest one before a new job
limitations: Pre-LLM; 'retain' needs judged outcomes or the case base fills with unvalidated solutions

title: Active Case-Based Reasoning for Lessons Delivery Systems
authors: Rosina Weber; David W. Aha; L. Karl Branting; J. Robert Lucas; Irma Becerra-Fernandez
key_findings: Most lessons-learned repositories are passive stand-alone systems that assume users have time, know where to look, can use the retrieval software and can interpret lessons
Authors' interviews suggest most military LL repositories are viewed by potential users as useless
Proposes active delivery: a monitor pushes the most relevant lessons into the decision process (HICAP planning); JULLS lessons had 43 attributes
practical_applications: Push the few most relevant lessons into the job's start step instead of hoping someone searches a log
limitations: Prototype demonstration, no controlled outcome study

title: Intelligent lessons learned systems
authors: Rosina Weber; David W. Aha; Irma Becerra-Fernandez
key_findings: (per search summary of the abstract) Studies show lesson-dissemination software does not effectively promote knowledge sharing; surveys LL processes, systems, design issues and AI support
practical_applications: Background for lesson capture + delivery design
limitations: Content not read; search snippet only

title: NASA: Better Mechanisms Needed for Sharing Lessons Learned (GAO-02-195)
authors: U.S. General Accounting Office
key_findings: Survey of 192 managers (115 usable): 23% had submitted a lesson to LLIS in 2 years, 43% had not; 27% unaware of LLIS; 58% cannot retrieve the right lessons at the right time; 53% found lessons useful <25% of the time
Barriers: no perceived benefit, intolerance of mistakes, fear of negative lessons, no time, hard to search ('weed through irrelevant lessons')
Recommendations: incentives, more positive lessons, mentoring/storytelling, better coding/search, user feedback, objective effectiveness metrics
practical_applications: Design for retrieval at the moment of need; include positive lessons; measure use

title: Review of NASA's Lessons Learned Information System (IG-12-012)
authors: NASA Office of Inspector General
key_findings: Only 16 of 28 project managers (57%) used LLIS; 12 of 28 (43%) contributed
Policy weakened: since 2007 lessons required only at closeout, not throughout the lifecycle; 8 of 10 Centers not fully compliant; 6 of 10 did not cross-reference lessons to standards
FY2011 cost $782,000; little correlation between funding and lessons contributed (JPL $70k -> 35 lessons vs Glenn ~$470k -> 5, FY2008-10)
LLIS marginalised in favour of Ask Magazine and seminars; users found it outdated, not user friendly
practical_applications: Capture lessons during the job, link each lesson to the standard/skill it changes, monitor use
limitations: Audit of one system; managers' self-report

title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I (Ch. 8 'History as Cause: Columbia and Challenger')
authors: Columbia Accident Investigation Board
key_findings: (per search summary) Board concluded the institutional causes of Challenger had not been fixed and saw 'echoes' of Challenger in Columbia; history treated as a cause
practical_applications: A lesson recorded is not a lesson learned until practice changes
limitations: Read only through search snippets; chapter not read this session

title: Site Reliability Engineering, Ch. 15: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure
authors: Google SRE (B. Beyer, C. Jones, J. Petoff, N. R. Murphy eds.)
key_findings: Blameless postmortem: focus on contributing causes; assume people acted on the information they had
Triggers defined in advance; contents: impact, mitigation, root causes, follow-up actions; reviewed by seniors; 'an unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed'
Kept in use via postmortem of the month, reading clubs, Wheel of Misfortune role-play, recognition, surveys
practical_applications: Define triggers for a studio review (user rejects, rerender >2x, quota wasted)

title: How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity
authors: Ed Catmull
key_findings: People learn from postmortems but dislike them, prefer to praise and move on, and 'game the system to avoid confronting the unpleasant'
Techniques: vary the postmortem format (same format finds the same lessons); each group lists top five things to do again and top five not to; use lots of data (rework rates, completeness at handoff)
Dailies: show unfinished work daily so people do not polish the wrong thing in private
practical_applications: Per job: keep-3 / change-3 with data (rerenders, quota used, user verdict)
limitations: Executive's own account; no independent evaluation

title: A Dynamic Theory of Organizational Knowledge Creation
authors: Ikujiro Nonaka
key_findings: Organisational knowledge is created through continuous dialogue between tacit and explicit knowledge; four patterns of interaction
New knowledge is developed by individuals; organisations articulate and amplify it
practical_applications: Plan how a tacit preference becomes an explicit rule, then a tool default, then habit

title: Conceptualizing Knowledge Creation: A Critique of Nonaka's Theory
authors: Stephen Gourlay
key_findings: Of SECI's four conversion modes three appear plausible but none is supported by evidence that cannot be explained more simply
Omits inherently tacit knowledge; radically subjective definition (knowledge in effect created by managers)
Proposes: non-reflective behaviour ~ tacit, reflective behaviour ~ explicit (after Dewey)
practical_applications: Keep examples (cases) beside rules; not all taste can be written down

title: Managing Knowledge in Organizations: A Nonaka's SECI Model Operationalization
authors: Maria Luisa Farnese; Barbara Barbieri; Antonio Chirumbolo; Gerardo Patriotta
key_findings: SECI modes: socialization (tacit-tacit), externalization (tacit-explicit), combination (explicit-explicit), internalization (explicit-tacit)
8-factor KMSP-Q (mentoring, knowledge sharing, team reflexivity, organizational memory, communication, technological support, HR training, HR development) validated on 372 + 466 employees
Reviews critiques: anecdotal evidence, hard to measure, limited predictive validity, cross-cultural generalisation questioned, tacit/explicit dichotomy vs continuum
practical_applications: Use the 8 dimensions as an audit list for the studio memory

title: The Tacit Dimension
authors: Michael Polanyi
key_findings: Bibliographic: origin of 'tacit knowledge' (reissued Univ. of Chicago Press 2009 with foreword by Amartya Sen; review record French 2010). Content cited only via Farnese 2019
practical_applications: Name the tacit layer: the user's 'feels right' judgments

title: Experiential Learning: Experience as the Source of Learning and Development
authors: David A. Kolb
key_findings: Bibliographic (existence confirmed via 1987 review record). Content stated only via Healey & Jenkins 2000 and Bergsteiner 2010

title: Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory and Its Application in Geography in Higher Education
authors: Mick Healey; Alan Jenkins
key_findings: Kolb's theory structures a session or course as a learning cycle; stages are associated with learning styles
practical_applications: Use the cycle as a session structure, not a personality type

title: Kolb's experiential learning model: critique from a modelling perspective
authors: Harald Bergsteiner; Gayle C. Avery; Ruth Neumann
key_findings: Kolb's graphical model shows graphic syntax errors, fails sufficiency/simplification tests, has categorisation and definition problems, misconstrued bi-polarities and flawed logic
practical_applications: Treat the Kolb cycle as a checklist, not a validated causal model

title: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence
authors: Harold Pashler; Mark A. McDaniel; Doug Rohrer; Robert A. Bjork
key_findings: Credible validation of learning-styles instruction (meshing hypothesis) requires classifying by style, random assignment to methods and a crossover interaction

Found virtually no evidence for that interaction; several adequate studies contradicted meshing; concluded no adequate evidence base for learning-styles assessment in general practice (many versions simply untested)
practical_applications: Do not tag lessons or users by 'learning style'; tag by task and failure mode

title: Single-Loop and Double-Loop Models in Research on Decision Making
authors: Chris Argyris
key_findings: An espoused theory of action based on single-loop learning is the most general model of action; a double-loop model gives feedback and more effective decisions
practical_applications: When the same fix recurs, question the governing rule or goal, not only the action

title: Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective
authors: Chris Argyris; Donald A. Schoen
key_findings: Bibliographic: foundational book on single/double-loop organisational learning (record confirmed; content not read)

title: Organizational Learning
authors: Barbara Levitt; James G. March
key_findings: Organisations learn by encoding inferences from history into routines that guide behaviour
Organisational memory: encoding, storage and retrieval of lessons despite turnover and time; limits of learning as intelligence
practical_applications: A lesson becomes organisational only when encoded in a routine (skill step, tool default)

title: Organizational Memory
authors: James P. Walsh; Gerardo R. Ungson
key_findings: Defines organisational memory and its structure; processes of acquisition, retention, retrieval; memory can be used, misused or abused
practical_applications: Map where studio memory lives: people, files, tools, routines

title: Learning Curves in Manufacturing
authors: Linda Argote; Dennis Epple
key_findings: Productivity rises with experience but learning rates vary greatly between organisations
Variation explained by organisational forgetting, turnover, knowledge transfer, economies of scale
practical_applications: Track a learning curve per job type (time or rerenders per accepted output)

title: The Acquisition, Transfer, and Depreciation of Knowledge in Service Organizations: Productivity in Franchises
authors: Eric D. Darr; Linda Argote; Dennis Epple
key_findings: 36 pizza stores, weekly data over 1.5 years: unit cost declines with experience
Knowledge acquired through learning by doing depreciates rapidly
Knowledge transfers across stores of the same franchisee but not across different franchisees
practical_applications: Lessons decay unless embedded; transfer works inside a connected group (same pipeline/skills)

title: Knowledge Management and Knowledge Management Systems: Conceptual Foundations and Research Issues
authors: Maryam Alavi; Dorothy E. Leidner
key_findings: KMS support creation, transfer and application of knowledge; process view of organisational KM and the role of IT
practical_applications: Design memory around create-store-transfer-apply, with 'apply' measured

title: Communities of Practice and Social Learning Systems
authors: Etienne Wenger
key_findings: Organisations succeed by designing themselves as social learning systems; three modes of belonging; communities of practice, boundary processes, identities
practical_applications: User + agents + skills as one community; shared files as boundary objects

title: Situated Learning: Legitimate Peripheral Participation
authors: Jean Lave; Etienne Wenger
key_findings: Learning is a social process; newcomers move from peripheral to full participation in a community of practice (midwives, tailors, quartermasters, butchers, recovering alcoholics)
practical_applications: New agents learn from worked examples of real past jobs

title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
authors: Amy C. Edmondson
key_findings: 51 work teams: team psychological safety associated with learning behaviour; team efficacy not, when controlling for safety
Learning behaviour mediates between psychological safety and team performance
practical_applications: Make it easy and safe for the user to say 'not this'; log the words without defending

title: Effects of feedback intervention on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
authors: Avraham N. Kluger; Angelo S. DeNisi
key_findings: 607 effect sizes: feedback improved performance on average (d=.41) but over one third of feedback interventions decreased performance
Effectiveness decreases as attention moves from the task toward the self
practical_applications: Lessons and critiques address the work, never the maker

title: A Meta-Analysis of Research on Hindsight Bias
authors: Rebecca L. Guilbault; Fred B. Bryant; Jennifer Howard Brockway; Emil J. Posavac
key_findings: 95 studies, 252 effect sizes: mean hindsight effect d=.39 (95% CI .36-.42)
Manipulations intended to reduce hindsight bias did not produce lower effect sizes
practical_applications: Write the expectation before the result so the review compares against a record, not memory

title: Outcome bias in decision evaluation
authors: Jonathan Baron; John C. Hershey
key_findings: Decision quality and decision-maker competence rated higher when outcomes were favourable, with identical information, even though subjects said outcomes should not count
practical_applications: Judge a choice by the information available at the time; one lucky viral post does not prove the recipe

title: Critical upward feedback in organisations: Processes, problems and implications for communication management
authors: Dennis Tourish; Paul Robson
key_findings: Health-care organisation (146 surveyed, 15 interviews, 6 focus groups): informal upward feedback mostly absent and inaccurately positive; senior managers unaware, overestimated how much they received, and discouraged critical feedback
practical_applications: Silence is not approval; ask a cheap, specific question

title: Understanding Organizational Practice Adoption at the Thai Subsidiary Corporation: Antecedents and Consequences of Kreng Jai
authors: Tim G. Andrews; Nartnalin Chompusri
key_findings: Qualitative study (interviews, observation, company documents) of a Thai subsidiary adopting European parent practices: e-communication, performance appraisal, empowerment
Kreng jai sometimes complements, reinforces, elaborates or contradicts what comparative cultural dimensions predict; ignoring it carries hidden risks
practical_applications: Capture feedback in ways that do not require blunt criticism (pick A/B, 1-5 rating)
limitations: Single case; abstract read via RePEc paraphrase

title: The construction of preference
authors: Paul Slovic
key_findings: Preferences are often constructed in the process of elicitation; normatively equivalent elicitation methods give systematically different responses (preference reversals)
practical_applications: Record how and in what context a preference was given; one answer is not a fixed taste

title: Collaborative Filtering for Implicit Feedback Datasets
authors: Yifan Hu; Yehuda Koren; Chris Volinsky
key_findings: Implicit feedback lacks direct evidence of dislikes; treat observations as positive/negative preference with widely varying confidence levels
practical_applications: Store a confidence with each taste record: explicit praise > used without comment > silence

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
authors: Patrick Lewis; Ethan Perez; Aleksandra Piktus; Fabio Petroni; Vladimir Karpukhin; et al.
key_findings: RAG combines parametric memory (seq2seq) with non-parametric memory (dense Wikipedia index); state of the art on three open-domain QA tasks
More specific, diverse and factual generation than a parametric-only baseline; provenance and updating knowledge named as open problems for parametric models
practical_applications: Keep studio knowledge in updatable files outside the model and cite them

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
authors: Nelson F. Liu; Kevin Lin; John Hewitt; Ashwin Paranjape; Michele Bevilacqua; Fabio Petroni; Percy Liang
key_findings: Performance often highest when relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input; degrades significantly when it is in the middle, even for long-context models
practical_applications: Put the few most relevant rules at the top of a brief; do not dump the whole memory
limitations: QA and key-value tasks; newer models may differ

title: Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
authors: Freda Shi; Xinyun Chen; Kanishka Misra; Nathan Scales; David Dohan; et al.
key_findings: GSM-IC: model accuracy dramatically decreases when irrelevant information is included; mitigations include self-consistency and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information
practical_applications: Retrieve few, relevant lessons; irrelevant lessons are not free

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
authors: Joon Sung Park; Joseph C. O'Brien; Carrie J. Cai; Meredith Ringel Morris; Percy Liang; Michael S. Bernstein
key_findings: Memory stream retrieval = recency (exponential decay 0.995 per game hour) + importance (LLM-rated 1-10) + relevance (embedding cosine), equal weights
Reflection triggered when summed importance of recent events exceeds 150 (about 2-3 times a day); reflections stored as memories citing evidence
TrueSkill believability (100 raters): full 29.89 > no reflection 26.88 > no reflection/planning 25.64 > human crowdworkers 22.95 > no memory 21.21
Failure modes: retrieval misses, embellishment (~1.3% of 453 relationship answers hallucinated), overly formal/cooperative behaviour, cost of thousands of dollars for 25 agents x 2 days
practical_applications: Score studio memories by recency + importance + relevance; periodic reflections with links to evidence
limitations: Measures believability, not correctness; sandbox; expensive

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
authors: Noah Shinn; Federico Cassano; Edward Berman; Ashwin Gopinath; Karthik Narasimhan; Shunyu Yao
key_findings: Actor + evaluator + self-reflection; verbal lessons kept in episodic memory (usually 1-3 reflections)
HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80.1% GPT-4; ALFWorld 130/134 tasks; but MBPP Python 77.1% vs 80.1% baseline
Limits: no gain on WebShop (needs diverse exploration); depends on evaluator quality (MBPP generated-test false positives 16.3% vs 1.4% HumanEval); no gain with a weaker model
practical_applications: A lesson loop works only with a trustworthy evaluator (user verdict, measurable check)

title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
authors: Jie Huang; Xinyun Chen; Swaroop Mishra; Huaixiu Steven Zheng; Adams Wei Yu; Xinying Song; Denny Zhou
key_findings: Without external feedback LLMs struggle to self-correct reasoning; performance sometimes degrades after self-correction
practical_applications: Do not let the agent write lessons from its own opinion alone; anchor on external signals

title: ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
authors: Andrew Zhao; Daniel Huang; Quentin Xu; Matthieu Lin; Yong-Jin Liu; Gao Huang
key_findings: Agent gathers experiences on training tasks, extracts natural-language insights, and recalls insights plus past experiences at inference; performance improves as experience accumulates
practical_applications: Two layers: raw cases + distilled insights

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
authors: Charles Packer; Sarah Wooders; Kevin Lin; Vivian Fang; Shishir G. Patil; Ion Stoica; Joseph E. Gonzalez
key_findings: Virtual context management: memory tiers paged into a limited context window, inspired by OS hierarchical memory; evaluated on large-document analysis and multi-session chat
practical_applications: Small always-loaded index; details paged in on demand

title: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents
authors: Theodore R. Sumers; Shunyu Yao; Karthik Narasimhan; Thomas L. Griffiths
key_findings: CoALA: language agents with modular memory components, a structured action space over internal memory and environment, and a decision process
practical_applications: Separate working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory

title: A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of Large Language Model based Agents
authors: Zeyu Zhang; Xiaohe Bo; Chen Ma; Rui Li; Xu Chen; et al.
key_findings: Survey: what agent memory is, why it is needed, how to design and evaluate it; limitations and future directions
practical_applications: Checklist for memory design and evaluation

title: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools
authors: Varun Magesh; Faiz Surani; Matthew Dahl; Mirac Suzgun; Christopher D. Manning; Daniel E. Ho
key_findings: Preregistered evaluation: RAG-based legal tools hallucinate less than GPT-4 but still 17-33% of the time; vendor 'hallucination-free' claims overstated
practical_applications: Retrieval reduces but does not remove invented facts; cite file paths and check

title: PROV-O: The PROV Ontology (W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013)
authors: W3C Provenance Working Group (T. Lebo, S. Sahoo, D. McGuinness eds.)
key_findings: Starting-point classes Entity, Activity, Agent; properties wasGeneratedBy, used, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, wasAssociatedWith
practical_applications: Each lesson/taste record notes output (entity), job (activity), judge (agent), and what it was derived from
limitations: Only the first part of the spec read

title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data
authors: European Parliament and Council of the EU
key_findings: Principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation ('adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary'); accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality
practical_applications: Store only what the purpose needs; no customer personal data in lessons; prune stale records
limitations: EU law; Thai PDPA is the local law but was not read this session
